pos: n. pl. (those who cut the fleece from sheep; the setting of Nabal's feast and the figure of Christ's silence)
etymology: Old English sceran, to cut. Sheepshearing was a festival as much as a labour — a season of plenty and open-handedness, which is why Nabal's refusal was so plainly an insult.
biblical_def: David sends to Nabal at the shearing: “I have heard that thou hast shearers: now thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them” (1Sa 25:7). Nabal answers with contempt — “Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse?” (1Sa 25:10) — and then, “Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?” (1Sa 25:11). Isaiah turns the same scene into the Servant's silence: “as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shearer as one that shears sheep, and shearing as the operation of clipping or cutting off the fleece.
webster_full: SHEARER, n. One that shears sheep or cloth.
SHEARING, n. The act or operation of clipping or cutting with shears; the fleece taken from a sheep at one time.
FLEECE, n. The coat of wool that covers a sheep, or is shorn off at one time.
scriptures: And now I have heard that thou hast shearers: now thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel.
And Nabal answered David's servants, and said, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master.
Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?
Isa 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 53:7 makes Christ's silence before His accusers a deliberate submission rather than a failure of defence.
corruption_paragraphs: A sheep under the shears does not struggle, and Isaiah chose the picture for a reason. Christ before Caiaphas held His peace; before Herod He answered nothing; before Pilate He answered never a word, insomuch that the governour marvelled greatly. He was not overwhelmed and He was not without a defence — He told Pilate plainly that he could have no power at all except it were given him from above. The silence was chosen, because the charge He was under was one He had come to bear. The eunuch was reading exactly this place when Philip found him: “like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth” (Act 8:32), and Philip preached unto him Jesus.

The corruption to name is any account of the cross as a tragedy that befell a good man, in which Christ is chiefly a victim of injustice. Injustice there certainly was, and the Gospels name it. But John 10:18 forecloses the reading: no man taketh my life from me, but I lay it down of myself; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. The silence at the trial and the willingness at Gethsemane are the same act. First Samuel 25 supplies the sharpest contrast to it — Nabal, whose name means fool, loud with his rights at his own shearing feast, and dead within ten days.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazaz (H1494), to shear, cut off; Greek keiro (G2751), to shear; Hebrew alam (H481), to be dumb, bind the tongue.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazaz (H1494) — to shear sheep, cut off; 1 Samuel 25:7, Genesis 31:19.
Hebrew alam (H481) — to be dumb, silent; Isaiah 53:7, Psalm 39:2, Ezekiel 3:26.
Greek keiro (G2751) — to shear, cut the hair; Acts 8:32, 18:18.
Hebrew nagas (H5065) — to oppress, exact; Isaiah 53:7, Exodus 3:7.
Hebrew nabal (H5036) — foolish, senseless; 1 Samuel 25:25, Psalm 14:1.
usage: “Thou hast shearers” — David's claim on a feast he had helped protect.
“Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse?” — Nabal's answer.
“As a sheep before her shearers is dumb” — the silence of the Servant.

pos: v. (worked dough with the hands; a labour of hospitality, of grief, and in Hosea of hidden sin)
etymology: Old English cnedan, to knead. Hebrew lush, to knead — a household verb, done quickly and by hand, and therefore the mark of a meal made in haste for a guest.
biblical_def: The witch of Endor feeds a doomed king: “she hasted, and killed it, and took flour, and kneaded it, and did bake unleavened bread thereof” (1Sa 28:24). Tamar bakes for Amnon at his request: “she took flour, and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight” (2Sa 13:8). Abraham does the same for the three men: “Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth” (Gen 18:6). And Hosea turns the baker's craft into a portrait of a nation's hidden corruption: “They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker, who ceaseth from raising after he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened” (Hos 7:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to knead as to work and press ingredients into a mass, usually with the hands, particularly to work flour or meal into a well mixed mass with water.
webster_full: KNEAD, v.t. To work and press ingredients into a mass, usually with the hands; particularly, to work into a well mixed mass the materials of bread, cake or paste.
KNEADING-TROUGH, n. A trough or tray in which dough is worked and mixed.
DOUGH, n. Paste of bread; a mass composed of flour or meal moistened and kneaded, but not baked.
scriptures: Gen 18:6
And Abraham hastened into the tent unto Sarah, and said, Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth.
And the woman had a fat calf in the house; and she hasted, and killed it, and took flour, and kneaded it, and did bake unleavened bread thereof:
So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house; and he was laid down. And she took flour, and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight, and did bake the cakes.
Hos 7:4
They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker, who ceaseth from raising after he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened.
corruption_summary: Hosea 7 describes sin working quietly in a nation the way leaven works in dough while the baker sleeps.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea's figure is exact and unpleasant. The baker kneads the dough at night, banks the oven, and sleeps; nothing appears to be happening; and in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire. The prophet is describing a nation whose corruption is fully prepared before it is visible — adulteries, conspiracies, drunken princes, all fermenting in the dark. Sin is patient in a way that alarms nobody until the morning. The same figure governs the New Testament warnings about leaven: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump, said twice by Paul, of doctrine in Galatians and of scandal in Corinth.

The corruption to name is the toleration of small compromises on the ground that nothing has visibly gone wrong. Hosea grants the premise — nothing has visibly gone wrong yet, the baker is asleep and the house is quiet — and says that is precisely the danger. Churches do not usually fall by a decision; they rise one morning and find that the oven is alight. The counter-image is Genesis 18, where Abraham hastens, Sarah kneads, and a meal is thrown together at speed for guests who turn out to be more than guests. Hospitality is hasty and honest; corruption takes its time.
roots_summary: Hebrew lush (H3888), to knead; qemach (H7058), meal, flour; chametz (H2557), leavened.
roots_lines: Hebrew lush (H3888) — to knead; Genesis 18:6, 1 Samuel 28:24, 2 Samuel 13:8, Hosea 7:4.
Hebrew qemach (H7058) — meal, flour; Genesis 18:6, 1 Kings 17:12.
Hebrew chametz (H2557) — leavened bread; Exodus 12:15, Hosea 7:4.
Hebrew matstsah (H4682) — unleavened bread; 1 Samuel 28:24, Exodus 12:39.
Greek zume (G2219) — leaven; 1 Corinthians 5:6, Galatians 5:9.
usage: “Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it” — Abraham's hospitality.
“She took flour, and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight” — Tamar before Amnon.
“After he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened” — Hosea on hidden sin.

pos: v. (to draw and twist fibre into thread; used by Christ of the labour the lilies do not perform)
etymology: Old English spinnan. Spinning was the constant domestic labour of the ancient household — the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31 lays her hands to the spindle — which is what makes Christ's illustration bite.
biblical_def: Christ names spinning only to set it aside. “And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Mat 6:28), “And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29). Luke records the same: “Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not” (Luk 12:27). And the argument is stated: “if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to spin as to draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or by machinery, and figuratively to draw out tediously.
webster_full: SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or by machinery; as, to spin wool, cotton or flax.
SPIN, v.t. To draw out tediously; to form by a slow process, or by degrees.
SPINDLE, n. The pin used in spinning wheels for twisting the thread.
scriptures: Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Mat 6:30
Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?
Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
corruption_summary: Christ's argument against anxiety is not that provision is unimportant but that the Father who clothes the grass will not fail His children.
corruption_paragraphs: The lilies argument is a lesser-to-greater proof and not a counsel of idleness. Christ does not tell men to stop spinning; He tells them to stop taking thought — the anxious, dividing care that the word carries. The reasoning runs: God clothes a wildflower with a glory Solomon could not match, and burns it in the oven tomorrow; you are worth more than grass and you are His child; therefore the anxiety is not humility but unbelief, and He names it — O ye of little faith. The same passage that forbids anxiety commands labour elsewhere in the plainest terms, and the two never collide because the object of anxiety is the future and the object of labour is today.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the cure for anxiety in Scripture is doctrine about God rather than technique. Christ argues; He does not soothe. He points to birds, to flowers, to the Father's knowledge of what we have need of, to the futility of adding a cubit by worry, and to the priority of the kingdom. Philippians 4 does the same — be careful for nothing, but by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. The peace comes after the argument and the prayer, and it comes from God rather than from a change of perspective.
roots_summary: Greek netho (G3514), to spin; merimnao (G3309), to be anxious, take thought; oligopistos (G3640), of little faith.
roots_lines: Greek netho (G3514) — to spin; Matthew 6:28, Luke 12:27 only.
Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, take thought; Matthew 6:28, 6:34, Philippians 4:6.
Greek oligopistos (G3640) — of little faith; Matthew 6:30, 8:26, 14:31.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to toil, labour to weariness; Matthew 6:28, John 4:38.
Hebrew tavah (H2901) — to spin; Exodus 35:25, 35:26.
usage: “They toil not, neither do they spin” — the lilies of the field.
“Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.”
“Shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” — the argument named.

pos: v. (formed on a loom without seam; of the priestly robe and of the coat of Christ)
etymology: Old English wefan, to weave. Woven work in Exodus is a single continuous fabric, made whole on the loom rather than cut and sewn — and that detail is the whole point of John 19.
biblical_def: The high priest's robe was made in one piece: “it shall have a binding of woven work round about the hole of it, as it were the hole of an habergeon, that it be not rent” (Exo 28:32), and it was made so — “he made the robe of the ephod of woven work, all of blue” (Exo 39:22), with “coats of fine linen of woven work for Aaron, and for his sons” (Exo 39:27). At the cross the soldiers meet the same kind of garment: “now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout” (Joh 19:23) — and they would not tear it, but cast lots, that the scripture might be fulfilled (Joh 19:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to weave as to unite threads of any kind in such a manner as to form cloth, and woven as formed by weaving, as distinguished from that which is sewed together.
webster_full: WEAVE, v.t. To unite threads of any kind in such a manner as to form cloth. This is done by crossing the threads by means of a shuttle.
WOVEN, pp. of weave. Formed by weaving or intertexture of threads.
SEAM, n. The suture or juncture of two edges of cloth sewed together.
scriptures: And there shall be an hole in the top of it, in the midst thereof: it shall have a binding of woven work round about the hole of it, as it were the hole of an habergeon, that it be not rent.
And he made the robe of the ephod of woven work, all of blue.
And they made coats of fine linen of woven work for Aaron, and for his sons,
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
corruption_summary: The priestly robe was made that it be not rent, and the priest who tore his own robe at the trial condemned himself out of his own vestment.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 28:32 gives a reason for the binding at the neck of the robe: that it be not rent. Leviticus 21:10 makes it law — the high priest shall not uncover his head nor rend his clothes. At the trial of Christ, Caiaphas rent his clothes and said, he hath spoken blasphemy. In the moment the true High Priest stood before him, the Aaronic high priest tore the garment he was forbidden to tear, and the seamless coat belonged to the man he was condemning. John notes that the soldiers would not rend that one. The old priesthood tore itself apart at the trial of the new, and the Epistle to the Hebrews spends thirteen chapters on the consequence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care with which the New Testament reads the ceremonial law. It does not allegorize freely; it follows the pattern God gave and shows it fulfilled in Christ — the veil, the mercy seat, the day of atonement, the Passover lamb, the seamless robe. Hebrews 10:1 states the hermeneutic: the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things. The shadows were designed. That is why a detail about a binding at a collar, given in Exodus for the sake of durability, turns up at Golgotha in the hands of four soldiers who did not know what they were holding.
roots_summary: Hebrew arag (H707), to weave; maaseh oreg, woven work; Greek huphantos (G5307), woven, made on a loom.
roots_lines: Hebrew arag (H707) — to weave; Exodus 28:32, Judges 16:13, Isaiah 59:5.
Greek huphantos (G5307) — woven; John 19:23 only.
Greek araphos (G729) — without seam; John 19:23 only.
Hebrew tachra (H8473) — habergeon, coat of mail; Exodus 28:32, 39:23.
Hebrew meil (H4598) — robe, mantle; Exodus 39:22, 1 Samuel 15:27.
usage: “That it be not rent” — the reason for the binding on the priestly robe.
“The robe of the ephod of woven work, all of blue” — made whole on the loom.
“Without seam, woven from the top throughout” — the coat at the cross.

pos: v. (braided, plaited; used only of the crown of thorns the soldiers wove for Christ)
etymology: From plat, a variant of plait, from Old French pleit, a fold. The Greek pleko is to twist or braid — a made thing, requiring time and care, which is what makes the crown of thorns so deliberate.
biblical_def: All three occurrences of the word describe the same act. “And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!” (Mat 27:29). Mark: “they clothed him with purple, and platted a crown of thorns, and put it about his head” (Mar 15:17). John: “the soldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put it on his head, and they put on him a purple robe” (Joh 19:2). The soldiers sat down and braided it. Mockery took effort.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to plat as to weave; to form by texture; and a plat as work done by platting or interweaving.
webster_full: PLAT, v.t. To weave; to form by texture. Matt. xxvii.
PLAIT, v.t. To fold; to double in narrow streaks; also, to braid; to interweave strands.
BRAID, v.t. To weave or intertwine three or more strands into one.
scriptures: And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
And they clothed him with purple, and platted a crown of thorns, and put it about his head,
Joh 19:2
And the soldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put it on his head, and they put on him a purple robe,

They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be: that the scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did.
corruption_summary: The soldiers crowned Christ with the curse of Genesis 3 and did not know they were staging the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Thorns entered the world by sentence: cursed is the ground for thy sake; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee. The soldiers platted that curse into a circle and pressed it on the head of the last Adam, then bowed the knee and called Him King. Every element of the mockery was accidentally true. He was the King; He was being crowned; and the crown was made of the very curse He had come to bear, of which Paul writes that He was made a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. They meant it for derision, and it was a coronation.

The corruption to name is the sentimentalizing of the passion, which turns the mockery into pathos and loses the doctrine. The crown of thorns is not primarily an image of Christ's suffering as such; it is an image of substitution. Ground cursed for Adam's sake yields the crown for Adam's Redeemer. The opposite error is equally common in another quarter — treating the physical agony as the whole of the atonement, when Scripture's emphasis falls on the wrath borne and the righteousness fulfilled. The thorns say both things at once: real blood, and a curse being carried away by the One it did not belong to.
roots_summary: Greek pleko (G4120), to plat, braid; stephanos (G4735), a crown, wreath; akantha (G173), thorn.
roots_lines: Greek pleko (G4120) — to plat, braid, weave; Matthew 27:29, Mark 15:17, John 19:2 only.
Greek stephanos (G4735) — crown, victor's wreath; Matthew 27:29, Revelation 2:10.
Greek akantha (G173) — thorn; Matthew 27:29, 13:7, Hebrews 6:8.
Greek empaizo (G1702) — to mock, deride; Matthew 27:29, 27:31, Luke 18:32.
Hebrew qots (H6975) — thorn; Genesis 3:18, 2 Samuel 23:6.
usage: “When they had platted a crown of thorns” — mockery that took effort.
“They bowed the knee before him, and mocked him” — every word of it true.
“They put on him a purple robe” — the colour of kings, in derision.

pos: adj. (smoothed and made to shine by working; of a shaft, of daughters, and of the appearance of glory)
etymology: Latin polire, to smooth. Polishing is subtractive work — the shine comes from what is removed — which is why Scripture uses it of things long prepared before they are used.
biblical_def: The Servant is a weapon kept out of sight until the hour: “he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me” (Isa 49:2). The psalmist prays for daughters “as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace” (Psa 144:12), and ends, “Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” (Psa 144:15). And Daniel describes the man by the river: “his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude” (Dan 10:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to polish as to make smooth and glossy, usually by friction, and figuratively to refine; to make elegant and polite.
webster_full: POLISH, v.t. To make smooth and glossy, usually by friction; as, to polish glass, marble or metal.
POLISH, v.t. To refine; to wear off rudeness, rusticity and coarseness; to make elegant and polite.
POLISHED, pp. Made smooth and glossy; refined.
scriptures: That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace:
Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD.
Isa 49:2
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;
Dan 10:6

His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
corruption_summary: The polished shaft spends most of its life in the quiver, and Isaiah offers the hiddenness as part of the preparation rather than a delay in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 49:2 is the servant's account of his own obscurity. The mouth is made a sharp sword and then hidden in the shadow of God's hand; the shaft is polished and then put in the quiver. Preparation and concealment are the same sentence. The pattern recurs everywhere in Scripture — Moses forty years in Midian, David in the wilderness with a kingdom already anointed on him, Paul in Arabia, Christ Himself thirty years in a carpenter's shop. The polishing is real work, done by friction, and it is done out of sight.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hiddenness is not wasted time, and its opposite — the drive to be visible early — is a besetting temptation of ministry in an age that can manufacture an audience before it has anything to say. Paul's rule for elders is that a novice must not be advanced, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil. Psalm 144 asks for children built like the polished corner stones of a palace, which is slow work on unseen surfaces. The shaft is not less a shaft while it is in the quiver.
roots_summary: Hebrew barar (H1305), to purify, make bright, polish; chets (H2671), arrow, shaft; ashpah (H827), quiver.
roots_lines: Hebrew barar (H1305) — to purify, make bright, polish; Isaiah 49:2, Daniel 12:10.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — arrow, shaft; Isaiah 49:2, Psalm 127:4.
Hebrew ashpah (H827) — quiver; Isaiah 49:2, Psalm 127:5, Job 39:23.
Hebrew chatab (H2404) — to hew, carve, polish; Psalm 144:12, Proverbs 7:16.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be burnished, polished; Daniel 10:6, Ezekiel 1:7.
usage: “Made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me” — preparation and hiding together.
“Our daughters may be as corner stones, polished” — the prayer of Psalm 144.
“Like in colour to polished brass” — the man Daniel saw by the river.

pos: v. (given an edge; of the sword of judgment and of the tongue used as a weapon)
etymology: Old English scearp, cutting. Hebrew chadad, to be sharp — the same root as the iron that sharpeneth iron in Proverbs 27:17, where the edge is given for good rather than for harm.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's sword song repeats the word like a hammer: “A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished” (Eze 21:9); “It is sharpened to make a sore slaughter; it is furbished that it may glitter” (Eze 21:10); “this sword is sharpened, and it is furbished, to give it into the hand of the slayer” (Eze 21:11) — and the prophet is told to grieve over it: “Cry and howl, son of man: for it shall be upon my people” (Eze 21:12). David uses the same verb of speech: “They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips” (Psa 140:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sharpen as to make sharp; to give a keen edge or fine point to; and figuratively to make more eager, keen, or severe.
webster_full: SHARPEN, v.t. To make sharp; to give a keen edge or fine point to; as, to sharpen a knife or an ax.
SHARPEN, v.t. To make more eager or active; to make keen or biting; as, to sharpen the appetite or a reproach.
FURBISH, v.t. To rub or scour to brightness; to polish; to burnish.
scriptures: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah.
Eze 21:9
Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus saith the LORD; Say, A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished:
It is sharpened to make a sore slaughter; it is furbished that it may glitter: should we then make mirth? it contemneth the rod of my son, as every tree.
Cry and howl, son of man: for it shall be upon my people, it shall be upon all the princes of Israel: terrors by reason of the sword shall be upon my people: smite therefore upon thy thigh.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel is commanded to preach the sword and to howl over it in the same breath, which is the whole standard for preaching judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 21 is the fiercest sword passage in the prophets, and God will not let the prophet deliver it coldly. Sigh, son of man, with the breaking of thy loins; cry and howl; smite upon thy thigh. The message is unsparing and the messenger is broken by it, and both are commanded. Jeremiah does the same — oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people. Christ pronounces the woes on Jerusalem in Matthew 23 and weeps over the city in the next chapter.

The corruption to name is preaching judgment without grief, which the pulpit has never been short of and which Ezekiel forbids by example. The doctrine of hell handled with satisfaction is the doctrine of hell misunderstood by the man handling it. The opposite failure is more common now — the silence that will not name the sword at all, and calls the silence compassion. God's own testimony settles which is the merciful course: as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live. That verse is a warning delivered with tears, and it is both.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadad (H2300), to be sharp, sharpen; marat (H4803), to furbish, make bright; shanan (H8150), to whet, sharpen.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadad (H2300) — to be sharp, sharpen; Ezekiel 21:9, 21:11, Proverbs 27:17.
Hebrew marat (H4803) — to furbish, scour bright; Ezekiel 21:9, 21:10, Isaiah 18:2.
Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to whet, sharpen, teach diligently; Psalm 140:3, Deuteronomy 6:7.
Hebrew chereb (H2719) — sword; Ezekiel 21:9, Genesis 3:24.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — poison, venom, fury; Psalm 140:3, Deuteronomy 32:24.
usage: “A sword, a sword is sharpened” — the refrain of Ezekiel 21.
“Cry and howl, son of man” — the manner commanded with the message.
“They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent” — speech as a weapon.

pos: v. (preserved a body with spices after the Egyptian manner; done in Scripture only to Jacob and Joseph)
etymology: Old French embaumer, from en- + basme, balm. The practice is Egyptian, and the Hebrew simply borrows the sense — to spice, to preserve with balm.
biblical_def: “And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father: and the physicians embalmed Israel” (Gen 50:2). “And forty days were fulfilled for him; for so are fulfilled the days of those which are embalmed: and the Egyptians mourned for him threescore and ten days” (Gen 50:3). And at the end of the book: “So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt” (Gen 50:26). Both men were embalmed for the same reason: neither intended to stay. Jacob had charged, “bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite” (Gen 49:29), and Joseph took an oath, “ye shall carry up my bones from hence” (Gen 50:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to embalm as to open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent putrefaction.
webster_full: EMBALM, v.t. To open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent its putrefaction.
EMBALM, v.t. To preserve from loss or decay, as reputation; to cherish the memory of.
BALM, n. The sap or juice of trees or shrubs remarkably odoriferous or aromatic.
scriptures: And he charged them, and said unto them, I am to be gathered unto my people: bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
Gen 50:2
And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father: and the physicians embalmed Israel.
And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.
So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
corruption_summary: Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt and a promise about bones, and Hebrews calls that arrangement an act of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The last verse of Genesis is a coffin. Joseph, the second man in Egypt, dies at a hundred and ten, is embalmed by the best craft in the world, and is laid in a box that will not be buried for four hundred years. Hebrews 11:22 identifies the faith in it precisely: By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones. He believed the promise so firmly that he made his own corpse a standing witness to it. Exodus 13:19 records Moses taking the bones, and Joshua 24:32 records the burial at Shechem, in the parcel of ground Jacob bought. It took four centuries and God kept it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith looks past the grave to a land it has not seen. The chapter that praises Joseph's bones says of the whole company that they died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Embalming preserved a body; the promise concerned a resurrection and an inheritance, and Joseph was reckoning on the second when he arranged the first. A Christian's dealings with death — how he buries, what he says over a grave — ought to say the same thing his creed says.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanat (H2590), to embalm, to spice; aron (H727), chest, coffin; etsem (H6106), bone.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanat (H2590) — to embalm, spice, ripen; Genesis 50:2, 50:3, 50:26.
Hebrew aron (H727) — chest, coffin, ark; Genesis 50:26, Exodus 25:10.
Hebrew etsem (H6106) — bone, substance; Genesis 50:25, Exodus 13:19, Ezekiel 37:1.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, number, attend to; Genesis 50:25, Exodus 3:16.
Greek exodos (G1841) — a departing, exodus; Hebrews 11:22, Luke 9:31.
usage: “The physicians embalmed Israel” — Jacob prepared for a journey home.
“Ye shall carry up my bones from hence” — Joseph's oath.
“He was put in a coffin in Egypt” — the last words of Genesis.

pos: v. (mingled in due proportion; of the meat offering, the holy perfume, and the members of the body of Christ)
etymology: Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion, to moderate. Tempering is proportion — not the presence of ingredients but their right measure, which is why Paul reaches for the word to describe the church.
biblical_def: The word belongs first to the sanctuary. Of the consecration bread: “cakes unleavened tempered with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil: of wheaten flour shalt thou make them” (Exo 29:2). Of the incense: “thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35), which was beaten small and set before the testimony “where I will meet with thee: it shall be unto you most holy” (Exo 30:36). And Paul carries it into the church: “God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked” (1Co 12:24), “That there should be no schism in the body” (1Co 12:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to temper as to mix so much as is proper; to qualify by mixture; to bring to a moderate state; and to compound or form by mixture.
webster_full: TEMPER, v.t. To mix so much as is proper; to qualify by mixture; as, to temper mortar.
TEMPER, v.t. To compound; to form by mixture; as, to temper a perfume.
TEMPER, v.t. To bring to a proper degree of hardness; as, to temper iron or steel.
scriptures: Exo 29:2
And unleavened bread, and cakes unleavened tempered with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil: of wheaten flour shalt thou make them.
And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy:
For our comely parts have no need: but God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked:
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
corruption_summary: Paul says God gave more abundant honour to the part that lacked, so the church's proportions are His arrangement and not a problem to be corrected.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 12 answers a congregation that ranked its members by gift. Paul's reply is that the body's proportions are tempered by God deliberately, and tempered against the instinct the Corinthians had: the parts that seem feeble are necessary, the parts we think less honourable receive the more abundant honour, and the whole arrangement exists that there should be no schism in the body. The comparison of gifts is destroyed at the root, because the distribution is the work of the Spirit dividing to every man severally as he will. The eye may not tell the hand it has no need of it; God tempered them together.

The corruption to name is the celebrity structure that the modern church has borrowed from the surrounding culture, in which visibility is the measure of value and the unseen members of a congregation are, in practice, its audience. Corinth had the same disease in a first-century form. The New Testament remedy is not to abolish the differences — Paul insists on them, are all apostles? are all prophets? — but to receive them as a tempering, with honour flowing toward the parts that lack it. Exodus supplies the older picture: the holy perfume was made by proportion, and the proportion was commanded, and no man was to make any like it for himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew balal (H1101), to mingle, temper with oil; mamlach (H4414), salted, tempered together; Greek sugkerannumi (G4786), to mix together, temper.
roots_lines: Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, mix with oil; Exodus 29:2, Leviticus 2:4.
Hebrew mamlach (H4414) — salted, tempered together; Exodus 30:35 only.
Greek sugkerannumi (G4786) — to mix together, temper; 1 Corinthians 12:24, Hebrews 4:2.
Greek schisma (G4978) — schism, division, rent; 1 Corinthians 12:25, 1:10, John 7:43.
Hebrew roqach (H7543) — to compound, as an apothecary; Exodus 30:35, 30:25.
usage: “Cakes unleavened tempered with oil” — the bread of consecration.
“A confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together” — the holy perfume.
“God hath tempered the body together” — the church's proportions are His.

pos: v. (washed with clean water; the second washing that finished a ceremonial cleansing)
etymology: Old French rincer, to wash. In Leviticus the rinsing is distinct from the scouring — the vessel is first scoured and then rinsed in water, and only then is it clean for use.
biblical_def: Of the vessel a sin offering was boiled in: “the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” (Lev 6:28). Of the man with an issue: “whomsoever he toucheth that hath the issue, and hath not rinsed his hands in water, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even” (Lev 15:11), and “the vessel of earth, that he toucheth… shall be broken: and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water” (Lev 15:12). The cleansing itself required time and running water: “he shall number to himself seven days for his cleansing… and bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean” (Lev 15:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to rinse as to wash; to cleanse by washing; and particularly to cleanse with a second or repeated application of water after washing.
webster_full: RINSE, v.t. To wash; to cleanse by washing.
RINSE, v.t. To cleanse with a second or repeated application of water, after washing; as, to rinse a vessel.
SCOUR, v.t. To rub hard with something rough, for the purpose of cleaning.
scriptures: Lev 6:28
But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water.
And whomsoever he toucheth that hath the issue, and hath not rinsed his hands in water, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even.
And the vessel of earth, that he toucheth which hath the issue, shall be broken: and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial washings could reach the vessel and the flesh, and Hebrews says the blood of Christ reaches the conscience, which they never could.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 15 is careful, repetitive, and physical: rinse the hands, wash the clothes, bathe the flesh, break the earthen vessel, count seven days, use running water. Hebrews 9 grants that all this sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, and then asks how much more shall the blood of Christ purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God. The old washings could not touch the conscience; that is the exact point of the argument, and it is why the sacrifices were repeated year by year continually. Hebrews 10:22 then takes the imagery over wholesale — hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and bodies washed with pure water — and calls the result full assurance of faith.

The corruption to name is the attempt to quiet a guilty conscience by any external means, which is the oldest religion in the world and is not confined to religious people. Ceremonies, resolutions, restitution, self-punishment, and the modern secular liturgies of self-improvement all promise to reach where Leviticus admitted it could not go. The gospel's claim is specific and exclusive: the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. Anything else scours the vessel. Only that rinses the man.
roots_summary: Hebrew shataph (H7857), to rinse, overflow, wash away; maraq (H4838), to scour, polish; mayim chayyim, living or running water.
roots_lines: Hebrew shataph (H7857) — to rinse, wash away, overflow; Leviticus 6:28, 15:11, Psalm 69:2.
Hebrew maraq (H4838) — to scour, furbish; Leviticus 6:28, 2 Chronicles 4:16.
Hebrew mayim chayyim — running, living water; Leviticus 15:13, Jeremiah 2:13.
Greek rhantizo (G4472) — to sprinkle; Hebrews 10:22, 9:13.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience; Hebrews 10:22, 9:14, 1 Peter 3:21.
usage: “It shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” — the brasen pot of the sin offering.
“Hath not rinsed his hands in water” — the touch that defiled.
“Our bodies washed with pure water” — the imagery taken up in Hebrews.
